children: is turning its delivery app into a broader food marketplace, adding Papa John's orders and challenging DoorDash
Customers can order Papa John's through Walmart's app or website for delivery in 30 minutes or less. They can also combine restaurant food with groceries and other Walmart products in a single order.

The bundling matters. Walmart says roughly 65% of existing restaurant-delivery orders already include merchandise from its stores, potentially increasing basket sizes while giving customers another reason to open its app.
Walmart Turns Store Proximity Into a Delivery Weapon

The partnership will begin in select U.S. markets within weeks before expanding to thousands of Papa John's locations. It is Walmart's third recent restaurant-delivery agreement, following Subway and Dunkin'.

Papa John's is the first participating chain that is not also a Walmart tenant. That marks an important shift from delivering food prepared inside stores toward competing as a general restaurant-delivery platform.

Walmart can lean on infrastructure it already built for e-commerce. Spark drivers, who operate as independent contractors, will handle deliveries. The retailer says 90% of Americans live within 10 miles of its more than 4,600 U.S. stores, creating a reach few competitors can match.

The service belongs to Walmart's express-delivery business, which charges a flat fee for orders arriving within an hour. Adding restaurant meals could improve driver utilization, increase order frequency and spread delivery costs across larger baskets.

For DoorDash and Uber Technologies, Walmart's expansion introduces a rival with enormous customer traffic, nearby inventory and its own delivery workforce. The challenge for Walmart is execution: delivering hot restaurant food alongside retail products within tight windows without compromising quality or margins. If it succeeds, a pizza partnership could become a much larger threat to established delivery apps.

title: Walmart Takes Direct Aim at DoorDash and Uber
